## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- transcribe and translate a sequence from either strand, and splice a pre-mRNA by hand using the GU…AG rule;
- predict whether skipping an exon keeps the reading frame;
- explain how promoter, splice-site, poly(A) and coding mutations differ in their effect on the gene product;
- reason through Crick and Brenner's frameshift combinations;
- find a gene's transcripts and **MANE Select** transcript in **Ensembl**, its protein isoforms in **UniProt**, and connect an isoform to an exon.

This is a recap of 5MO103, so the exercise is short.

## Background

**Transcription.** RNA polymerase II starts at the promoter (TATA box about 25–30 bp upstream). The mRNA has the sequence of the **coding strand** (U for T) and is complementary to the **template strand**.

**Processing.** A 5′ cap is added; the RNA is cut after an **AAUAAA** signal and given a poly(A) tail; **introns** are removed by the spliceosome. An intron starts with **GU** (donor) and ends with **AG** (acceptor), with a **branch-point A** upstream of the AG.

**Reading frame.** Translation starts at AUG and continues in one frame until a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA). Skipping an exon whose length is a **multiple of 3** keeps the frame; otherwise the frame shifts. A premature stop codon well before the last exon–exon junction triggers **nonsense-mediated decay** (NMD).

**The code** is triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate and nearly universal. Frameshift combinations (Crick and Brenner): (+)(−) or (+)(+)(+) close together restore the frame.

**Codon numbering.** In a coding sequence, codon *n* covers c.(3*n*−2) to c.3*n*.

## By hand

**B1. (strands)** The *HBB* coding strand starts 5′-`ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGAGGAG`-3′.

a) Write the template strand, 5′ → 3′.
b) Write the mRNA and translate it.
c) An RNA polymerase moves along the template strand. In which direction (3′ → 5′ or 5′ → 3′ of the template)?

**B2. (splicing by hand)** An invented pre-mRNA contains two exons and one intron:

`AUGGCCAAGGUAAGUGACUAACUUUUCCUUUCAGGAAUUCUGGUAA`

The first exon is `AUGGCCAAG`.

a) Find the intron using the GU…AG rule. How long is it?
b) Write the spliced mRNA and translate it.
c) A mutation changes the first base of the intron from G to A, and the intron is no longer removed. Translate the unspliced RNA. What happens to the protein?

**B3. (in frame or not?)** The *CFTR* MANE Select transcript (Ensembl 116) has these exon lengths for exons 9–13:

| exon | 9 | 10 | 11 | 12 | 13 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| length (nt) | 93 | 183 | 192 | 95 | 87 |

a) For each exon, would skipping it keep the reading frame?
b) The cystic fibrosis allele c.1585-1G>A destroys the acceptor site of exon 12. If this leads to skipping of exon 12, what happens to the protein?

**B4. (Crick and Brenner)** Predict wild type or mutant for each combination of proflavin-induced frameshifts, all close together near the start of the gene: a) (+)(+); b) (−)(−)(−); c) (+)(−)(+); d) (+)(+)(+)(+); e) (+)(+)(−)(−). Explain the rule.

**B5. (properties of the code)**

a) Why can the code not be a doublet code (2 bases per amino acid)?
b) If codons **overlapped** (bases 1–3, 2–4, 3–5, …), how many amino acids would a single base change alter? What does HbS (one amino acid changed) tell you?

**B6. (six mutations, one gene)** For each *HBB* variant from the lecture, say whether a patient's haemoglobin would contain an **abnormal β-globin**, a **reduced amount** of normal β-globin, or **no** β-globin from that allele:

a) c.-78A>C (TATA box); b) c.20A>T (HbS); c) c.92+1G>A (splice donor); d) c.93-21G>A (new acceptor); e) c.118C>T (nonsense); f) c.*111A>G (poly(A) signal).

## Find it

[Ensembl](https://www.ensembl.org/Homo_sapiens/Info/Index) shows each gene with all its annotated transcripts; [UniProt](https://www.uniprot.org/) shows the proteins, including **isoforms** made by alternative splicing. Both change between releases: this exercise was written with **Ensembl release 116** (check the release number at the bottom of any Ensembl page).

**F1. (transcripts in Ensembl)** Open the Ensembl gene page for [*CFTR* (ENSG00000001626)](https://www.ensembl.org/Homo_sapiens/Gene/Summary?g=ENSG00000001626).

a) On which chromosome and which strand is *CFTR*?
b) Click **Show transcript table**. How many transcripts are there? Which one is tagged **MANE Select**, and which RefSeq transcript does it match?
c) Click the MANE Select transcript ID. In its summary, read the number of exons, the transcript length (bp) and the protein length (aa).

**F2. (isoforms in UniProt)** Open [UniProt P13569](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P13569/entry) (CFTR_HUMAN) and go to the **Sequence & Isoforms** section.

a) How many isoforms are listed, and how long is the canonical isoform?
b) How does isoform 2 differ from isoform 1, and how long is it?

**F3. (which exon?)** Isoform 2 lacks amino acids 404–464.

a) Which coding positions (c.) encode codons 404–464?
b) Coding position c.1 lies in exon 1, and exons 1–9 contain 1209 coding nucleotides in total. Which exon encodes c.1210 onwards? Use B3: where does that exon end? So which exon does isoform 2 lack?

**F4. (a splicing mutation in ClinVar)** Open the ClinVar record [VCV000007112](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/variation/7112/) (or search ClinVar for `CFTR[gene] AND c.1585-1G>A`). Read the HGVS name, the **molecular consequence**, the classification and the dbSNP ID. Which exon's splice site does it hit, and which nonsense allele from the mutation unit lies in the same exon?

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions: By hand"}

**B1.** a) Reverse complement: 5′-**`CTCCTCAGGAGTCAGATGCACCAT`**-3′.
b) mRNA 5′-`AUGGUGCAUCUGACUCCUGAGGAG`-3′: **Met Val His Leu Thr Pro Glu Glu**.
c) The polymerase makes RNA 5′ → 3′, so it moves along the template **3′ → 5′**.

**B2.** a) The intron starts at the first GU after the exon (`GUAAGU…`) and ends at the AG before `GAAUUC`: **`GUAAGUGACUAACUUUUCCUUUCAG`**, 25 nt.
b) Spliced: `AUG GCC AAG GAA UUC UGG UAA`: **Met Ala Lys Glu Phe Trp Stop**.
c) Unspliced, with the mutation: `AUG GCC AAG AUA AGU GAC UAA`: **Met Ala Lys Ile Ser Asp Stop**. The intron is read as if it were coding, and contains a stop codon three codons in: a short, non-functional protein (and in a real cell the mRNA would likely be destroyed by NMD). (The sequence is invented.)

**B3.** a) 93 = 3 × 31: **in frame**. 183 = 3 × 61: **in frame**. 192 = 3 × 64: **in frame**. 95 = 3 × 31 + 2: **frameshift**. 87 = 3 × 29: **in frame**.
b) Skipping exon 12 (95 nt) shifts the reading frame after exon 11. The following codons are misread until a premature stop codon appears, and the mRNA is likely destroyed by NMD: a **null** allele, like G542X, which lies in the same exon.

**B4.** a) (+)(+): net +2: **mutant**. b) (−)(−)(−): net −3: **wild type** (one amino acid fewer). c) (+)(−)(+): net +1: **mutant**. d) (+)(+)(+)(+): net +4 = one codon plus +1: **mutant**. e) (+)(+)(−)(−): net 0: **wild type**. The rule: the frame is restored downstream when the net change is a **multiple of 3**. Only the short stretch between the first and last change is misread.

**B5.** a) 4^2^ = 16 doublets are too few for 20 amino acids. Triplets give 4^3^ = 64, enough (with degeneracy and stops).
b) With overlapping triplets, each base would belong to three codons, so one change would alter up to **three adjacent** amino acids. HbS, and other missense alleles, change exactly one amino acid, so codons do **not** overlap.

**B6.** a) **Reduced**: less transcription of a normal gene (β^+^). b) **Abnormal**: β-globin with Val instead of Glu (HbS). c) **None**: no normal splicing (β^0^). d) **Reduced**: most mRNA is mis-spliced, but some normal mRNA is made (β^+^). e) **None**: premature stop, mRNA destroyed by NMD (β^0^). f) **Reduced**: poor 3′-end processing gives less stable mRNA (β^+^). Only the missense change gives an abnormal protein; the other five are thalassaemias, diseases of **quantity**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions: Find it"}

These facts were checked with the Ensembl REST API (release 116), the UniProt REST API and NCBI E-utilities on 2026-11-20.

**F1.** a) Chromosome **7**, **forward** (+) strand (band 7q31.2). The location line gives the span of all transcripts together (7:117,287,120–117,715,971 in release 116).
b) **45 transcripts** in release 116 (other releases may differ). MANE Select: **ENST00000003084** (CFTR-201), matching RefSeq **NM_000492.4**.
c) **27 exons**, transcript length **6,070 bp**, protein **1,480 aa**. Click path: gene page → Show transcript table → click ENST00000003084 → transcript summary (or the **Exons** link in the left menu).

**F2.** a) **3 isoforms**; the canonical isoform 1 is **1,480 aa**.
b) Isoform 2 **lacks residues 404–464** ("Missing" in the Sequence & Isoforms section, or the alternative-sequence feature VSP_022123), and is **1,419 aa** long (1480 − 61). (Isoform 3, 604 aa, differs at the end from residue 589.)

**F3.** a) Codon 404 starts at c.(3 × 404 − 2) = **c.1210**; codon 464 ends at c.(3 × 464) = **c.1392**. So c.1210–c.1392, 183 nt.
b) c.1210 is the first base of **exon 10**, and exon 10 is 183 nt long (B3), so it ends at c.1392. Isoform 2 lacks **exactly exon 10**: an in-frame exon skip. (The R exercise finds the same with the exon table: the Ensembl transcript CFTR-218, 1,419 aa, has every MANE exon except exon 10.)

**F4.** **NM_000492.4(CFTR):c.1585-1G>A**, molecular consequence **splice acceptor variant**, classification **pathogenic** (review status: practice guideline), condition cystic fibrosis, dbSNP **rs76713772**. c.1585-1 is the last base of intron 11, the G of the AG right before **exon 12** (exon 12 starts at c.1585: 1209 + 183 + 192 = 1584 coding nucleotides in exons 1–11). G542X (c.1624G>T) lies in the same exon. (Its legacy name is 1717-1G>A, from an older numbering of the cDNA.)
:::

## Where this leads

This unit closes Part 3. You have seen how a gene is stored (DNA recap), how it changes (Mutation & complementation) and how it is read (this unit). **Part 4: Genome analysis** turns to the tools: finding genes and open reading frames in raw sequence, sequencing, and browsing variation across whole genomes. The idea of a gene as exons, introns and alternative transcripts is what a genome browser draws for you.

**Next:** [Exercise in R](exercise-r.qmd): load the exon table of all *CFTR* transcripts, compute exon and transcript lengths with `group_by()` and `summarise()`, find the exon that isoform 2 lacks, and draw the transcripts with `geom_segment()`.
